newsitem.title: FRANCE: Clinton backs bigger NATO role for France, Europe.
newsitem.headline: Clinton backs bigger NATO role for France, Europe.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton said on Thursday that he backed a European initiative for a separate defence pillar within NATO and favoured giving more command responsiblity to Paris within the alliance.
But he again ruled out giving up NATO's southern command to a European, the price set by France for its full return to the NATO military command structure.
"It wouldn't from my point of view be a sensible thing to do militarily," he told France 3 television in an interview conducted at the White House.

France has said the United States should hand over NATO's southern command, which controls the Mediterranean, to the Europeans as its price for rejoining the integrated military structure it quit in 1966 saying the alliance was dominated by Washington.
Clinton, in the interview, sounded conciliatory towards Paris, which has formally ruled out returning fully to NATO ahead of a July 8-9 NATO summit in Madrid.
Paris also slammed Washington this week over its decision to limit to three the number of eastern European states to be invited in Madrid to join an expanded alliance.

Washington wants the first wave of new NATO states to include only the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland while France and some of its European allies want two more on the list -- Romania and Slovenia.
Clinton said NATO expansion would resume in two years and said he was committed to helping other nations to qualify for membership.
He also urged France as well as Spain to return soon to NATO's military command.

"I want greater command responsibilities to be given to the Europeans and I have supported that. The United States has favoured integration of France and Spain, has favoured the European defence initiative within NATO and more responsiblity to the French," he said.
Asked about French charges of U.S. "hegemony" in world affairs," Clinton said he and France were partners who worked together closely.
"All I can say is that I do not want America to dictate its conduct to Europe," he said, noting that the United States has worse poverty and poorer health care than European states.
In response to a question, Clinton also said he was not bothered by the presence of communists in France's new leftist government.
Former U.S. president Ronald Reagan was angered when the late French head of state Francois Mitterrand named communists to his government in 1981.
